Aerial Wildlife 
Survey Report 
Provincial Pronghorn Antelope Survey Summary 2017 
 
Background 
Aerial surveys for pronghorn antelope have been conducted annually in Alberta since 1963. In 1985 , a trend block 
survey was developed to sample portions of primary range in each Antelope Management Area (AMA) in the 
province, although every AMA was not flown in each year (see Table 1 for Wildlife Management Units [WMUs] 
and area of each AMA).  
 
In 1996, rotary-wing replaced fixed-wing surveys and most AMAs have been surveyed annually since that time. 
Approximately 17% of the 37,544 km2 of primary antelope range in the province is surveyed to provide information 
on population densities and herd composition both within AMAs and provincially.  
 
From 2007 to 2012, antelope surveys were conducted by the Alberta Conservation Association (ACA) and 
summary results can be found on their website at: 
 Big Game Surveys 
https://www.ab-conservation.com/programs/wildlife/big-game-surveys  
Pronghorn antelope hunting opportunities are in high demand in Alberta, making the information collected during 
annual surveys a critical component of pronghorn management. This report provides detailed results of surveys 
conducted by Alberta Environment and Parks (AEP) in 2017 and summarizes provincial pronghorn survey trends 
from 2007 to 2017. 
 
Survey method 
Surveys were flown in a Bell 206B from July 4 to 13, 2017. Each Antelope Management Area contains from 1 to 7 
designated survey blocks with 1.6 kilometre wide fixed strip transects. At each observation point animals were 
counted and classified as bucks, does or kids. The antelope density (#/km 2) of the surveyed area within each 
AMA was calculated by dividing the number of animals observed on transect by search area (sum of transect 
lengths multiplied by 1.6 kilometres) and multiplying by the overall area of primary range in the AMA.  
 
For a population estimate within each AMA, the overall number observed was divided by overall area surveyed 
and multiplied by the area of the AMA. The estimated provincial population was the sum of all AMA survey 
estimates, and did not include pronghorn occupying CFB Suffield (AMA S) at the time of the survey. CFB Suffield 
was last surveyed in 2009 where 2,469 pronghorn (10% of the provincial population) were estimated to occur.  
 
AMA G and H also contain expanses of secondary range that are not surveyed. Populations  in secondary range 
are estimated as 0.04/km2 multiplied by the area of secondary range in AMA G and H. The population split of 
buck, doe, and kid for each AMA was calculated by multiplying the total estimated population by the proportion of 
each age/sex class observed. Provincial estimates for buck and kid to doe ratios were calculated by totals of each 
age/sex class summed across AMAs (i.e. buck:doe ratio=total bucks/total does; kid:doe ratio=total kids/total 
does).

Results 
In 2017, the total survey effort was 5,905 km2 of an estimated 37,544 km2 (16%) of primary pronghorn antelope 
range in AMA A-H. Secondary range in AMA G and H is approximately 2,121 km2 and 9,098 km2, respectively. 
That contributes an estimated 82 animals to the overall estimate in AMA G, and 351 animals to the estimate in 
AMA H.  
 
In total, 2,826 pronghorn were observed on-transect; 1,460 does, 619 bucks, and 747 kids. The provincial 
buck:doe and kid:doe ratios were 0.42 and 0.51, respectively. The provincial estimate was 18,185 with a 
population split of 9,409 doe, 3,954 buck, 4,822 kid. The highest population density occurred in AMA C and A, 
while buck:doe and kid:doe ratios were highest in AMA A and B, respectively (Table 2). 
Between 2009 and 2011 the provincial pronghorn antelope population was estimated to decline 42% from 20,111 
to 11,701 animals; the population in 2011 was the lowest on record since 1996. Between 2011 and 2014, the 
population increased by an estimated 3,624 animals (15%/year). A slight decline was observed in the herd 
between 2014 and 2015 (Table 3). Between 2015 and 2017 the population increased  23%, roughly 12%/year. 
Further, kid:doe ratios were the highest observed in the last 10 years, indicating good recruitment in 2017.
